Unit Economics

Contribution margin at the level of one unit is arithmetic that a competent analyst can finish in ten minutes. What separates an expert is knowing that the arithmetic is the least interesting part: every serious disagreement about unit economics is a disagreement about a counterfactual, a horizon and a unit — never about the subtraction.

1. Two rooms, two decisions, one question

On Monday 9 February 2026, in a converted warehouse off Hosur Road in Bengaluru, Vikram Iyer was preparing a recommendation he had been avoiding for six weeks. Iyer was Senior Vice President of Product at Lakshit Diagnostics Systems, an eleven-year-old company that made a bench-top point-of-care immunoassay analyser and the single-use cartridges that ran on it. Lakshit's machines sat in roughly 3,100 diagnostic laboratories, nursing homes and small hospitals across India, most of them outside the metros, running thyroid panels, cardiac markers and infection assays that would otherwise have been couriered to a reference lab in a district town two hours away. The company sold the analyser outright for ₹3,60,000 and then sold cartridges at ₹185 each, forever.

The commercial team wanted to stop doing that. Abbott, Roche and Siemens Healthineers had for years placed instruments free of charge in Indian labs under what the industry calls reagent rental — the lab pays nothing for the box and commits instead to a minimum monthly consumption of the manufacturer's consumables at a higher unit price. Lakshit's sales head had modelled the switch and produced a single, arresting slide: under placement, the lifetime contribution from an average installed analyser rose from ₹11.5 lakh to ₹16.8 lakh. A 45 per cent improvement, achieved by giving the hardware away. Sunita Rao, the CFO, had circulated the slide with a one-line question attached: whose average? Iyer had until the board's 26 February meeting to answer her, and he suspected the answer would cost the commercial team its favourite slide.

Eight hundred kilometres north-west, in a glass tower in HITEC City, Hyderabad, Nandita Sundaram was three days from a signature she did not want to give. Sundaram was Chief Product Officer of Lavanaya Systems, a four-year-old company whose product read insurance claim documents, extracted the facts, checked them against policy terms and produced an adjudication recommendation with a cited justification. Lavanaya had spent nine months in a paid pilot with one of India's five largest general insurers. The pilot had been a success by every measure the insurer tracked: turnaround time on cashless pre-authorisation had fallen from nineteen hours to fifty-one minutes, and the insurer's own audit found Lavanaya's recommendation materially correct on 99.7 per cent of sampled claims. The insurer now wanted a three-year enterprise agreement covering its entire claims book — roughly nine lakh claims a year — at a flat ₹42 per claim.

Lavanaya's own numbers said the deal was excellent. Cost to serve a claim during the pilot had averaged ₹19.95. At ₹42, that was a 52.5 per cent contribution margin, comfortably inside what Lavanaya's investors expected of a software company, and the contract would take the company past ₹40 crore of annual recurring revenue. Sundaram's problem was that she had spent the previous fortnight pulling the cost distribution rather than the cost average, and what she found was that the median claim in the pilot had cost Lavanaya ₹4.90 while the ninety-ninth percentile claim had cost ₹118 — and that the pilot had run exclusively on structured, machine-readable health pre-authorisations, which were the cheapest eleven per cent of the book the contract would now cover.

Iyer and Sundaram were asking the same question in different currencies. Both had a per-unit contribution number that was arithmetically correct and decisionally useless, and both had arrived at that number by the same route: they had computed an average across a population that the decision in front of them was about to change. The rest of this page is an argument that this is not an accident of two badly-run analyses but the characteristic failure of unit economics as it is practised, and that the discipline's real content lies in three questions the arithmetic never asks — what is the unit, which costs would actually disappear if that unit disappeared, and over what horizon.

Unit economics is not a measurement. It is a counterfactual claim: if this one unit had not existed, these rupees would not have been spent, within this window of time. Everything that makes the subject difficult — step costs, shared costs, density effects, stochastic costs, risk provisions, organisational seams — is a way in which that counterfactual is harder to establish than it looks.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about what

Begin with the definition, stated more carefully than it usually is. The unit economics of a business is the contribution margin attributable to one instance of a chosen unit — a customer, an order, an installed machine, an adjudicated claim, a delivered kilogram — where contribution margin is the revenue the unit generates less the costs that would not have been incurred had the unit not existed, assessed over a stated horizon. Three clauses in that sentence do all the work and are routinely dropped. A chosen unit: the choice is a judgement, not a fact about the business. Costs that would not have been incurred: avoidability, not the label "variable" in the chart of accounts. Over a stated horizon: almost every cost is avoidable if the horizon is long enough, and almost none is avoidable if it is short enough.

The arithmetic is old. John Maurice Clark's Studies in the Economics of Overhead Costs, published in 1923, gave the field its governing maxim — different costs for different purposes — and made the argument that an allocated share of overhead is the wrong number for almost every operating decision a manager faces. The cost-volume-profit machinery that followed in American management accounting through the 1930s and 1940s, and which Charles Horngren codified for two generations of MBA students from 1962 onward, is the direct ancestor of the spreadsheet a product manager builds today. What the twentieth century called contribution analysis, the twenty-first calls unit economics; the subtraction has not changed.

What changed was who was asking and why. After the 2000 dot-com collapse, venture investors who had funded companies that grew revenue impressively while losing money on every incremental transaction began demanding order-level arithmetic as a condition of financing, and by the mid-2010s writers such as Bill Gurley and David Skok had made the vocabulary standard. In India the phrase entered boardroom currency during the 2015–2023 funding cycle, when the question put to founders in diligence shifted from how large the business was to whether a single transaction, unsubsidised, made sense. That history matters because it explains a persistent confusion: the management-accounting tradition invented per-unit contribution to answer operating questions — should we accept this order, drop this SKU, run this shift — and the venture tradition repurposed it to answer an investment question, whether the model will eventually earn a return. The two traditions use the same arithmetic to answer questions that have different correct answers, and a great deal of what looks like disagreement about unit economics is two people quietly answering different questions.

There are, in practice, five positions a well-informed practitioner might hold. They are not shades of one view; they make incompatible recommendations in identifiable situations, and it is worth knowing precisely what each will and will not sign.

3. Mechanics in depth: the four steps that are usually left implicit

Step one: choose the unit, and justify it with a counterfactual

Most treatments say "choose the unit that matches your business" and move on. The operative test is sharper. A candidate unit is valid if you can complete this sentence with something you could verify: if one of these had not happened, the following rupees would not have been spent, within the following number of weeks. For Lakshit the tempting unit is the cartridge, because cartridges are what customers buy repeatedly. It is the wrong unit. The decision Iyer faces changes how analysers are placed, not how cartridges are consumed; a cartridge's avoidable cost is ₹96 of materials and nothing else, which tells him nothing about whether to give away a ₹2,10,000 machine. The correct unit is the installed analyser over its contracted life, because that is the object whose existence or non-existence determines the ₹2,28,000 of hardware and installation, the thirty-six months of field service, and the entire cartridge stream. For Lavanaya the tempting unit is the claim; the correct unit, as will become clear, is the claim of a given type, because cost varies by a factor of twenty-four across types and the contract mixes them.

Step two: sort costs by avoidability and horizon, not by the ledger's labels

The familiar three-bucket sort — variable, semi-fixed, fixed — is a shorthand for a two-dimensional question that experts hold explicitly: for each cost line, is it avoidable if this unit vanishes, and how long would it take to avoid? A field engineer's salary is unavoidable this week and entirely avoidable over a year. Reserved cloud capacity is unavoidable for the duration of the commitment and then wholly avoidable. A regional depot's lease is unavoidable for its term and avoidable at renewal. Drawing this as a matrix, rather than as a three-way sort, prevents the single most common technical error in the subject, which is to quote a per-unit cost without stating the horizon at which it was computed and then to compare it with a number computed at a different horizon.

Two analysts who disagree about whether a business has "positive unit economics" are usually standing in different columns of this figure without saying so.

Step three: write the cost function, not the cost number

The formal treatment that experts carry in their heads, and rarely write down, is that contribution margin is a function rather than a scalar. In the simplest case it is affine in the size of the unit: contribution equals a variable contribution rate multiplied by the unit's rupee value, less the flat per-unit costs. That is the version most product managers eventually internalise. The version that separates practitioners is what happens when the function is not affine, and there are three important departures.

The first is step costs. A field engineer covers up to 180 analysers in a territory; the 181st installation adds an entire engineer. Modelled as a smooth per-unit cost, this produces a forecast in which unit economics improve continuously with scale; modelled honestly, it produces a saw-tooth in which economics improve until a threshold and then snap back. The tell is a five-year plan in which cost per unit declines along a smooth curve. Real cost per unit descends a staircase, and the height of the next step is usually knowable in advance.

The second, and the more consequential, is non-separability. Standard unit economics assumes that total contribution equals the number of units multiplied by the contribution of one unit — that units are independent. In any business with density effects this is false, and the error it produces is systematic rather than random. Consider Lalit Freight Exchange, a Nashik-headquartered marketplace matching shippers with fleet owners on full-truckload lanes, which will serve as this page's third case. Lalit pays fleet owners a supply incentive to keep trucks available on a lane, and the incentive it must pay falls as the lane gets busier, because a busier lane offers a truck a better chance of a return load. Suppose on a given lane the incentive per load is approximately ₹935 minus ₹0.35 for every load per month on that lane, so that at 900 loads a month the incentive is ₹620. Suppose revenue less all other per-load costs is ₹1,974. Then average contribution per load at 900 loads is ₹1,354.

The marginal load, however, is worth considerably more. Adding a load not only earns its own ₹1,354; it also reduces by ₹0.35 the incentive payable on all 900 existing loads, a further ₹315. Formally, if total contribution is T(N) = N·(r − s(N)) then the marginal contribution is r − s(N) − N·s′(N), and since s′ is negative the marginal exceeds the average. At 900 loads a month, the marginal load is worth ₹1,669 against an average of ₹1,354 — twenty-three per cent more. A company that evaluates lane investments at average contribution will systematically under-invest in exactly the dense lanes where investment pays best, and a company in a congestion-prone business, where the sign of s′ flips, will do the opposite and over-invest.

The dashed red line shows the error made by treating the supply incentive as corporate overhead rather than a per-load cost: it flatters every lane equally and destroys the information that would tell Lalit which lanes to invest in.

Step four: adjust for risk, cash and asymmetry before you call it contribution

Three adjustments separate a serious model from a naive one, and each is routinely skipped. The first is risk. A unit's contribution is an expectation over outcomes, not a certainty: some analysers are repossessed, some claims are wrong, some shippers default. Provisioning for the tail at the unit level, rather than discovering it in a separate line eighteen months later, is what makes unit economics comparable across cohorts with different risk profiles. The second is cash. Contribution margin is an accrual concept; a unit can be contribution-positive and cash-negative for a long time if inventory sits, receivables stretch or the hardware is funded upfront. The third is asymmetry. The management-accounting literature on cost stickiness — Anderson, Banker and Janakiraman's 2003 study of selling and administrative costs is the standard reference — found that costs rise substantially more when activity increases than they fall when activity decreases by the same amount. In plain terms, the "variable" costs in a downside scenario are less variable than the model assumes. Any unit-economics model that flexes costs symmetrically around the plan is optimistic by construction on the downside.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Unit economics earns its keep when four conditions hold, and each can be checked rather than assumed. Claim one: a meaningful share of total cost is attributable to individual units at the decision's horizon. For Lakshit this is emphatically true — hardware, cartridge materials and service together are the overwhelming majority of cost, and all three attach to an identifiable analyser. For Lavanaya it is true at the margin but less true in total: inference and human review attach to claims, but Lavanaya's model-adaptation team and its committed cloud capacity do not, and at current volumes those are a third of cash cost. Claim two: the units are approximately separable. True for Lakshit, where one lab's analyser does not affect another's costs. False for Lalit, as Figure 2 showed, and the falsity is the whole point of the business. Claim three: the population is homogeneous enough that an average is informative, or you are willing to compute the distribution. False for both protagonists, which is precisely why both are in trouble. Claim four: the observed unit cost is exogenous rather than a control variable. True for Lakshit's cartridge materials. Dramatically false for Lavanaya, whose per-claim cost is set by a confidence threshold that its own product team chooses.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. The first is a business whose costs are genuinely almost all fixed — a media property, a piece of pure software with no support obligation, a research tool. Here contribution margin is near ninety-nine per cent for every unit and the number carries no information; the real question is whether the fixed cost is ever recovered, which is a different calculation. The second is a business in the middle of a deliberate, temporary subsidy whose purpose is to buy an asset that does not appear in the unit's revenue — a network, a habit, a regulatory licence, a dataset. Measuring unit economics there without valuing the asset being purchased will condemn every investment ever made. The third is a capacity-constrained business at full utilisation, where the throughput school's objection bites: the correct question is not the margin of a unit but the margin per hour of the constrained resource, and a unit with an excellent margin that consumes six hours of a bottleneck may be worse than one with a thin margin that consumes ten minutes.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product: the costs no unit will ever carry

When two products share infrastructure, the sum of what each product would incrementally cost is less than what the two cost together, and the difference is unallocatable by any method that is both non-arbitrary and additive. Suppose Lakshit's cloud platform, which stores results, pushes NABL-compliant reports and manages instrument telemetry, costs ₹1.40 crore a year to run for both the immunoassay and the newer haematology line. Run for immunoassay alone it would cost ₹1.05 crore; for haematology alone, ₹0.95 crore. The incremental cost of haematology, given immunoassay, is ₹0.45 crore; the incremental cost of immunoassay, given haematology, is ₹0.35 crore. Those two incremental costs sum to ₹0.80 crore, leaving ₹0.60 crore — forty-three per cent of the platform — that belongs to neither product in any causal sense.

It is also, importantly, the wrong number for an operating decision. If the question is whether to discontinue haematology, the relevant figure is ₹0.45 crore, not ₹0.65 crore, because that is what would actually stop being spent. The mature practice is to maintain both: an incremental view for decisions about adding or dropping, and an allocated view for accountability and pricing floors, with an explicit line in the accountability view labelled "unallocated shared platform" so that nobody mistakes the sum of the product P&Ls for the company's P&L.

Two-sided markets: which side is the unit?

Lalit Freight Exchange illustrates the hardest version. A shipper's load and a fleet owner's truck are two sides of the same transaction; the company collects a take rate from one and often pays an incentive to the other. Computing unit economics per shipper makes the supply incentive look like a cost of acquiring shippers; computing it per fleet owner makes the take rate look like the revenue of a truck. Neither is wrong, and a company that reports both without reconciling them will double-count or double-subtract. The coherent unit in a two-sided business is the matched transaction, with cross-side subsidies shown explicitly as a transfer rather than netted away. The second-order complication is that the cross-side subsidy is an investment in liquidity with a decaying cost, exactly as Figure 2 showed, so a fixed per-transaction subsidy figure will be stale within two quarters in a growing lane and dangerously stale in a shrinking one.

Regulated businesses: the cost of capital held against the unit

In lending, insurance and payments, a unit consumes regulatory capital, and that capital has a cost that no chart of accounts will present as a cost of the unit. An insurer bound by IRDAI solvency requirements, or a lender operating under the RBI's digital-lending framework, must hold capital against each policy or loan; the return required on that capital is a genuine per-unit economic cost even though it appears in the accounts as equity, not expense. The tell that a model has missed it is a fintech business whose unit economics look identical to a software business's — contribution of seventy per cent and no capital line — while its balance sheet grows in proportion to volume. Practitioners in these industries handle it by computing a risk-adjusted return on capital per unit rather than a contribution margin, and product managers moving into regulated categories from software frequently take a year to absorb that the arithmetic they know is missing a term.

Hardware plus software: the unit that creates a liability

Lakshit's analyser makes the point vividly. Selling a machine does not merely convert inventory into revenue; it creates a three-year obligation to service that machine, calibrate it, ship spares, and host its data. Contribution that ignores the accrued service reserve overstates the sale. Worse, the reserve is not a constant: the failure rate of an analyser depends on where it is installed, and Lakshit's own field data showed that machines in coastal humidity and in locations with unstable power failed at nearly twice the rate of those in air-conditioned metro labs. A single per-unit service cost blends a ₹1,900-a-month machine with a ₹4,100-a-month machine, and since the cheap installations were disproportionately in the metros where the capital-sale model already worked, the blended figure was biased in favour of exactly the expansion that would worsen it.

AI-native products: a cost that is stochastic, endogenous and moving

Lavanaya's cost per claim is unusual in three ways simultaneously. It is stochastic: two claims of the same nominal type can differ eightfold in cost depending on document length, handwriting quality and whether the model escalates. It is endogenous: the escalation rate and the human-review rate are set by a confidence threshold that Lavanaya chooses, so per-unit cost is a point selected on a cost–quality frontier rather than a fact discovered about the world. And it is non-stationary: token prices for the frontier models Lavanaya calls had fallen by roughly seventy per cent over fourteen months, while Lavanaya's token consumption per claim had risen by rather more than that as the team added retrieval over policy wordings and multi-pass verification. Cost per claim had in fact increased slightly. The lesson generalises beyond AI but is sharpest there: when input prices fall, teams spend the saving on quality, and the unit cost curve you extrapolate is the product of two moving quantities pointing in opposite directions.

What happens at the organisational seams

The most expensive failures in this subject are organisational rather than analytical. A cost that is real, per-unit and growing will be omitted from a unit-economics model with near-certainty if it is owned by a different function, reported on a different cadence and lands in a different cost centre. Lalit's credit losses, discussed below, sat in a financial-services subsidiary that closed its books ninety days after the marketplace did. Lavanaya's human reviewers were staffed by an operations group that reported to the COO and was budgeted annually as headcount, so the product team's per-claim model carried inference cost to two decimal places and reviewer cost as a round number that had not been revisited in three quarters. Mature companies do not solve this by exhortation. They solve it by making the unit-economics model a single owned artefact with a named owner, by forcing every cost centre above a threshold to declare a driver — the thing that, if it doubled, would double that cost — and by auditing quarterly whether each declared driver is actually the one moving.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A unit economic is a counterfactual, and if nobody can state the counterfactual, the number is decoration. The tell-tale sign is a meeting in which somebody says "our cost per order is ₹86" and nobody asks over what period those ₹86 would stop being spent. The obvious reading is that cost per unit is a measurement, like weight. It is not; it is a conditional forecast about what a cost base would do under a change that has not happened. The practical consequence is that the same business can honestly report two very different unit economics to two audiences — an operating number for the next quarter's decisions and a steady-state number for a five-year investment case — and the sin is not having two numbers but failing to label which is which.

Marginal and average contribution are different quantities, and in any business with density or congestion they diverge materially. The tell is a model in which total contribution is computed as volume multiplied by per-unit contribution. The obvious reading — that the average is a reasonable proxy for the marginal — holds only when units are independent, which is exactly the assumption that network, logistics, marketplace and capacity businesses violate by design. An expert asked "what is the contribution of an order?" will ask back "the average order, or the next one?", and will expect the answer to differ by double digits.

Cost variability is asymmetric: costs climb faster than they fall. The tell is a downside scenario in which the cost base flexes at the same rate as the upside. Managers do not fire a field engineer the week volume dips, they do not release reserved cloud capacity mid-term, and they do not shrink a reviewer pool they expect to need next quarter. The obvious reading is that "variable cost" is a symmetric property of a cost line. In practice the asymmetry means a business whose unit economics look robust at plan can degrade sharply at eighty per cent of plan, and the diagnostic is to ask what the cost base actually did the last time volume fell — a question the finance team can answer from history in an afternoon.

When the cost distribution is skewed, the mean is the wrong summary and pricing against it is a structural error. The tell is a unit cost quoted without a percentile beside it. Lavanaya's mean of ₹19.95 sat at roughly the seventy-eighth percentile of its own distribution, meaning that the typical claim was four times cheaper than the average claim and that the average was a fact about the tail rather than about ordinary work. The obvious reading is that the mean is the right number because total cost equals mean times volume — which is true, and irrelevant, because the mix is not stable and the contract does not sample from the same distribution the pilot did.

In many modern products the per-unit cost is a choice, not a fact — a selected point on a cost–quality frontier. The tell is that nobody in the room can tell you the numerical value of the threshold that governs it. At Lavanaya the review rate was set by a confidence cut-off; moving that cut-off to send seventeen per cent of claims to human review rather than twenty-nine per cent would save ₹11.40 per claim and raise the material-error rate from 0.31 to 0.74 per cent, which at an average leakage of ₹4,800 per material error and a fifty per cent contractual pass-back would cost ₹10.32 per claim. The saving is ₹1.08. The obvious reading — that there is slack in the cost stack waiting to be cut — is wrong precisely because the team had already optimised: near an optimum the frontier is flat, and the existence of a flat frontier is itself the finding. Real improvement has to come from moving the frontier, not sliding along it.

Accrual contribution and cash contribution are different, and the gap can be large enough to kill a company with excellent unit economics. The tell is contribution margin improving while the cash conversion cycle lengthens. Under Lakshit's placement model, each installation consumed ₹2,28,000 of cash on day one and returned ₹16,330 a month at the volume of a typical Tier-2 lab: a fourteen-month payback per unit, during which the unit is contribution-positive and cash-negative. Scaling a business like that is a financing decision disguised as a pricing decision, and the obvious reading — that improving contribution margin improves the business — inverts when growth is fast enough that cash consumption outruns the balance sheet.

The tail belongs in the unit, provisioned in advance, not discovered later in a different line. The tell is a provision that is a plug, a bad-debt line that moves in round numbers, or a warranty accrual set by policy rather than by observed failure. Fraud, default, returns, repossession, liability and rework are all costs of serving a unit; the fact that they arrive stochastically and late does not make them less attributable. The obvious reading is that such costs belong to risk management. They belong to both, and the version the product team carries should be an expected value per unit with a stated distribution, not a footnote.

The average customer does not exist, and the cumulative contribution curve is usually shaped like a whale. The tell is a company that has never plotted cumulative contribution against customers sorted from best to worst. In Kaplan's classic finding, and in most cost-to-serve studies since, the top fifth of customers generate well over one hundred per cent of total contribution and the bottom decile destroys a meaningful fraction of it. Lakshit's installed base ran from seventy tests a month at the lower quartile to four hundred and eighty at the upper — a factor of nearly seven, on a decision whose break-even sat at one hundred and forty-three. The obvious reading is that a skewed distribution simply means some customers are better than others. The sharper reading is that a blanket policy applied to a skewed population is almost always value-destroying at one end, and that the design question is segmentation, not optimisation.

Revenue per unit is not price. The tell is a gap between list ARPU and cash collected per unit that nobody has decomposed. Discounts, promotional credits, refunds, service-level penalties, partial-period churn, channel margin and, in India, the difference between a composite and a mixed supply for GST purposes all sit between the two, and each is a real reduction in the unit's revenue. The obvious reading is that these are finance's problem. They are the product manager's problem the moment a packaging change alters the mix between them — Lakshit's shift from selling a device to bundling a device with a service, for instance, changes the applicable indirect-tax treatment and with it several points of realised margin, which is the kind of thing that is discovered after launch by companies that did not ask.

Improving margin per unit and improving total contribution are different objectives, and optimising the ratio can destroy the rupees. The tell is a team with a per-unit margin target rather than a contribution target. Raising a price, tightening eligibility or removing a low-margin SKU all reliably improve the ratio; whether they improve the total depends on elasticity, which unit economics alone cannot tell you. This is the single most common way in which a technically correct unit-economics exercise leads to a worse business, and it is why this topic hands off directly to price elasticity and willingness to pay.

Positive unit economics says nothing about whether the business earns its cost of capital. The tell is a model with a healthy contribution margin in which the words "invested capital" never appear. A business can be contribution-positive at every unit, cover its fixed costs, report an accounting profit, and still destroy value because the capital tied up in inventory, placed hardware, receivables and regulatory reserves earns less than it costs. The obvious reading — that unit economics is the foundation and everything else is superstructure — is right about the order of operations and wrong about the standard of proof.

7. How the picture changes by product type and by stage

Across product types the differences are real but narrower than the folklore suggests. In consumer transactional businesses the levers are basket size, fulfilment cost per trip and discount intensity, and the distinguishing feature is that units are numerous, cheap and highly heterogeneous, so the analysis is statistical from the outset. In B2B software the unit is the account rather than the transaction, cost of goods sold is small, and the dominant per-unit cost is the sales and success effort required to win and keep the account — which is why B2B unit economics is inseparable from customer acquisition cost and why a B2B company with a ninety per cent gross margin can still have catastrophic unit economics. In enterprise software the further twist is that the units are so few, and so different from one another, that averaging is nearly meaningless: a company with forty customers has forty unit economics, and the correct artefact is an account-level contribution table, not a blended metric.

Platforms and marketplaces differ in kind rather than degree, for the reason Figure 2 gave: their units are not independent, cross-side subsidy is a design choice rather than an accident, and the right unit is the matched transaction. Hardware and physical-goods businesses differ because a unit creates an obligation and consumes working capital, so contribution must be net of a service reserve and assessed alongside cash payback. AI products differ because cost per unit is stochastic, endogenous and non-stationary, and because a genuine debate exists about whether human review in the loop is cost of goods sold or a bridge that will be engineered away — a debate this page returns to below.

Where the difference is often asserted and is not real: people claim that pure-software businesses have no unit economics because marginal cost is zero. They have unit economics; the unit is the customer and the variable costs are support, success, payment processing and infrastructure, which in practice run between ten and thirty per cent of revenue for most B2B software and are anything but zero. People also claim that subscription businesses cannot use per-transaction analysis. They can and should; the transaction is the renewal.

Stage changes the practice more than product type does. At the earliest stage, when semi-fixed costs are absurdly oversized relative to volume — one field engineer for eleven analysers — the honest practice is to report today's actual unit economics and a clearly-labelled steady-state model side by side, with the assumptions that bridge them named and each one assigned to somebody who will be held to it. At growth stage, the discipline shifts to cohorts: the blended number becomes actively misleading, because a blend of an improving old cohort and a deteriorating new one can look flat for several quarters while the business inverts underneath. At maturity, the fixed-versus-variable line must be redrawn strictly and costs a startup could reasonably ignore are pushed down to the unit for accountability, which is why large companies often appear to have worse unit economics than their smaller competitors when in fact they merely have more honest ones.

8. Three worked examples

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs and the cost of catching them late

The first and most common failure is reporting gross margin and calling it unit economics. The early warning sign is a unit-economics slide that looks reassuring beside a cash-burn slide that does not. The diagnostic question is simple and nearly always productive: list every cost the company incurs that would not exist if this unit did not exist, and point to where each one appears in the reported margin. Caught in a quarter it is an embarrassment; caught after a financing round priced on the number, it is a governance problem.

The second is pricing off a mean drawn from a non-representative population — Lavanaya's situation exactly. The warning sign is a pilot whose scope was chosen by the customer for ease of integration rather than by the vendor for representativeness. The diagnostic question is: what is the distribution of the driver in the pilot, and what is it in the population the contract covers? Caught before signature it costs a fortnight of renegotiation; caught in year two of a three-year fixed-price contract it costs the contract's entire margin and usually the account team's credibility.

The third is the cost that lives in another cost centre. The warning sign is any per-unit cost owned by a function that does not attend the unit-economics review. The diagnostic question is whether any cost line in the company has grown more than proportionally with volume over eight quarters without appearing in the per-unit model. Lalit caught this after seven quarters; the cost was roughly ₹31 crore of contribution that had been reported and did not exist.

The fourth is treating a step cost as smoothly variable. The warning sign is a forecast in which cost per unit declines along a clean curve. The diagnostic is to plot historical cost per unit against historical volume and look for the staircase. Caught early it changes a hiring plan; caught late it produces the familiar pattern in which a company hits its volume target and misses its margin target in the same quarter, and cannot explain why.

The fifth is importing a mature market's assumptions into a new one. Delivery density, basket size, reviewer productivity, failure rates and discount intensity all differ by geography and segment, and importing them silently imports the old market's break-even point. The diagnostic is to demand that every assumption in a new-market model be sourced from that market or explicitly flagged as inherited. The cost of catching this late is measured in opened locations.

The sixth is optimising the ratio instead of the rupees. The warning sign is a team whose objective is expressed as a percentage. The diagnostic question is what happened to total contribution, in rupees, over the same period the margin improved. This failure is particularly insidious because it produces a chart that goes up and to the right while the business shrinks.

The seventh is letting the unit definition drift. Companies quietly redefine the unit when the old definition stops flattering — from contribution after all delivery costs to contribution after "core" delivery costs, from all customers to customers past their first ninety days. The warning sign is a footnote change in a metric definition without a restated history. The diagnostic is to recompute the current quarter on last year's definition. The cost of catching this late is that nobody in the company trusts any historical series.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does customer acquisition cost belong inside unit economics? The venture position is that it plainly does: a customer who cost ₹8,000 to acquire and returns ₹6,000 of lifetime contribution is a loss, and excluding acquisition cost allows a company to manufacture attractive unit economics by spending unboundedly on marketing. The contribution-accounting position is that acquisition spend is an investment in an intangible asset with a multi-period life, that treating it as a period cost of the units acquired in that period conflates capital and operating decisions, and that the resulting metric is unstable — cut marketing and unit economics "improve" instantly while the business decays. Both are right about the failure they fear. The practical resolution most sophisticated operators adopt is to compute two numbers and never blend them: contribution margin excluding acquisition, which governs operating decisions, and payback on acquisition, which governs growth-investment decisions. For this to be wrong, it would have to be the case that operating and investment decisions cannot be separated — which is in fact true in businesses where the product is the acquisition channel, and where the cleanest practitioners admit the framework strains.

Is anything other than materials genuinely variable? Goldratt's throughput accounting holds that labour, support and infrastructure are operating expense — bought in lumps, not consumed by the unit — and that contribution per unit of the binding constraint is the only per-unit metric with content. The evidence it rests on is strong in manufacturing and increasingly relevant to AI, where reserved capacity means the true marginal cost of an inference at low utilisation is close to zero and at high utilisation is the price of the next reserved block, not the list token price. The opposing, fully-burdened position rests on the observation that over any horizon long enough to matter, all those lumps are chosen in proportion to volume, and that a company which never charges units for lumpy costs simply never sees them. What would have to be true for the throughput view to be wrong: that capacity is genuinely purchasable in small increments at a constant price, which cloud pricing makes truer every year and committed-use discounts make less true.

Should an early-stage company model steady-state unit economics or today's? The steady-state camp points to the long list of businesses — semiconductor fabrication, electric vehicles, cloud infrastructure — whose early per-unit costs were catastrophic and whose learning curves were real and predictable. The today's-costs camp points to the far longer list of businesses in the 2021–2023 cohort whose steady-state model assumed a cost decline that never arrived, and observes that the steady-state assumption is unfalsifiable on any timescale short enough to be useful. The honest position, which neither camp states as a compromise, is that steady-state modelling is legitimate exactly to the extent that the mechanism of the cost decline is named, quantified and observable in-sample. "Costs will fall with scale" is not a mechanism. "Cost per install falls because an engineer covers 180 machines and we are at 61, and here is the observed cost curve across our three largest territories" is.

Is human review in an AI product cost of goods sold or a temporary bridge? One camp books reviewer cost as COGS, reports the resulting fifty per cent gross margin, and argues that a business should be valued on what it costs to run, not on what someone hopes it will cost. The other treats review as a transitional expense being actively engineered away, points to a declining review rate as evidence, and argues that capitalising the transition is no different from any other product investment. This disagreement is live, consequential and currently unresolved: it determines whether a large class of AI companies are software businesses with software multiples or services businesses with services multiples. What would have to be true for the bridge view to be right is that the review rate declines on a durable curve rather than asymptoting — and the uncomfortable evidence is that in several categories the review rate has fallen for eighteen months and then stopped, because the residual cases are residual for reasons that are not about model capability.

Does unit economics have content for zero-marginal-cost goods? The sceptical position is that for a pure software or media product the per-unit framework is a category error imported from manufacturing, and that the real questions are fixed-cost recovery and audience scale. The opposing position is that the sceptic has chosen the wrong unit: the unit is the customer, not the copy, and the variable costs of a customer — support, success, payments, infrastructure, compliance — are far from zero and are precisely where such businesses fail. Both sides are describing real companies. The reconciliation, such as it is, is that the framework's content scales with the share of cost that attaches to units, and that for a business where that share is under ten per cent, unit economics is a hygiene check rather than a strategy.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this subject produces a number. Someone who has internalised it produces a function, a distribution and a horizon, and treats the number as the least durable of the three. The behavioural differences are visible within about ten minutes of any serious conversation.

They ask what the unit is before they ask what the margin is, and they will change the unit mid-analysis when the decision changes. They are unembarrassed about maintaining two or three simultaneous unit-economics views of the same business for different questions, and they label each one with the question it answers. They quote percentiles beside means as a matter of habit, and their first instinct on being handed an average is to ask for the distribution behind it. They distinguish reflexively between the average and the next unit, and in density businesses they will say so unprompted. They know which of their cost lines are step functions and roughly where the next step sits. They ask what happened the last time volume fell, rather than assuming symmetry. They can name, for each significant cost centre, the driver that would double it. They treat every provision — warranty, default, rework, leakage — as a per-unit expected value with a distribution, not as a plug. They are deeply suspicious of a unit-economics improvement that coincides with a definition change, and they recompute on the old definition before they believe it. And when a model shows a business that works, they ask the question the contribution framework cannot answer: what capital is tied up in each unit, and does the return on it exceed what that capital costs.

The deepest marker is comfort with ambiguity of a specific kind. An expert will say, without discomfort, that the business has excellent unit economics on a one-year horizon and unproven ones on a five-year horizon, that the top two quintiles of accounts are outstanding and the bottom quintile is value-destroying, and that these statements are all simultaneously true and not in tension. The competent practitioner, pressed for a single verdict, will give one.

12. What Iyer and Sundaram decided

Iyer went to Lakshit's board on 26 February with a recommendation that satisfied nobody in the room initially. He proposed neither adopting placement nor rejecting it, but segmenting on observed volume — which Lakshit could do with unusual confidence, because its analysers reported their own test counts by telemetry, so eligibility could be based on measured history rather than a lab's forecast. Accounts running above 200 tests a month, comfortably clear of the 168-test risk-adjusted break-even, would be offered placement. Accounts below 140 would continue to be sold instruments outright. Between the two, a hybrid with a ₹1,20,000 refundable deposit and an intermediate cartridge price would recover the hardware cost within nine months regardless of volume. Every placed asset would carry a service reserve and a repossession haircut on the books, and the sales team's incentive would be paid on lifetime contribution rather than on placements. His argument to the board was not that the commercial team's number was wrong but that it was an average of a bimodal population, and that the single most valuable thing Lakshit owned in this decision was the telemetry that let it price the two modes separately.

Sundaram declined the flat ₹42 and proposed a three-tier schedule instead: ₹19 for structured pre-authorisation claims, ₹58 for reimbursement claims with unstructured discharge documentation, and ₹96 for motor third-party claims, with a volume-weighted collar so that the insurer's total cost at its stated mix landed within four per cent of the flat-rate proposal it had asked for. She added a re-price clause at nine months tied to two published indices — the observed mix and Lavanaya's measured escalation rate — and, in exchange, offered the insurer a share of any reduction in review rate that Lavanaya achieved. The headline contract value was eleven per cent below what the flat rate would have produced. Her argument internally, to a sales organisation that did not want to hear it, was that a flat price across a heterogeneous population is not a simplification but a bet that the mix will not move, and that Lavanaya had no information advantage on that bet and every incentive against it. The insurer's procurement team took five weeks and signed the tiered schedule.

Discussion questions

  1. Iyer's segmentation depends on telemetry that reveals each lab's true volume. Suppose that data did not exist and eligibility had to rest on the lab's own forecast. What would placement's break-even volume have to be, and what contract structure would you design, to make the scheme robust to a customer who systematically overstates?
  2. Sundaram's tiered pricing pushes mix risk back to the insurer, who arguably understands its own book better than Lavanaya does. Is that an efficient allocation of risk, or has Lavanaya simply declined to develop the one capability — predicting claim complexity from the claim's first page — that would let it price flat and win on cost?
  3. Lalit's blended contribution figure was accurate for seven quarters and wrong in every quarter. If you were joining as head of product, what single artefact would you demand in your first month to detect an equivalent problem, and what would prevent that artefact from being quietly redefined a year later?

13. Going deeper

  1. Contribution margin — the single subtraction this whole topic generalises; go back to it if the fixed–variable boundary still feels arbitrary, because everything above is an argument about where that boundary sits.
  2. CAC, LTV and payback — the direct extension when the unit becomes the customer rather than the transaction; it unlocks the growth-investment half of the argument in section ten.
  3. Forecasting demand and revenue — unit economics is a function of volume, so any forward-looking verdict is only as good as the volume forecast underneath it, including its step-cost thresholds.
  4. Price elasticity and willingness to pay — the missing term whenever someone proposes to fix unit economics by raising price; it tells you whether the ratio improves at the cost of the rupees.
  5. What a business model is — places unit economics inside the larger structure of how value is created, delivered and captured, and explains why a subsidised unit can be rational.
  6. Subsidies and incentive design — the formal treatment of Lalit's supply incentive: when a deliberately negative unit economic is buying an asset, and how to tell when it has stopped.
  7. Reading a P&L — the reconciliation skill; you cannot defend a unit-economics number in a board meeting unless you can walk it to the statutory statements.
  8. Gross margin and cost to serve — the distinction section nine's first failure mode turns on, and the activity-based machinery for computing cost to serve at customer level.
  9. Cash flow, burn and runway — the accrual-versus-cash nuance in operational form; Lakshit's fourteen-month payback is a runway question disguised as a pricing question.
  10. SaaS metrics: ARR, MRR, churn, NRR — how the per-unit frame is expressed in subscription businesses, and why net revenue retention is a unit economic with a time dimension folded in.
  11. Market sizing (TAM / SAM / SOM) — the other half of the investment question: a beautiful unit economic in a market of four thousand units is a lifestyle business.
  12. Fermi estimation — the skill that lets you build a defensible unit-economics model in twenty minutes with no data, which is the situation you will most often be in.

Unit Economics

Does the business make money one order at a time — before anyone adds up the whole company?

1. A dark store in Nagpur, and a number that will not hold still

On the second Tuesday of April 2026, Ananya Kelkar sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of Girija Mart's Pune headquarters, staring at a spreadsheet that would decide whether the company opened twelve new dark stores in Nagpur by August. Girija Mart delivered groceries to customers' doors in under fifteen minutes, competing directly with Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart in a category where every large player was still spending investor money faster than it collected revenue from customers. Ananya was the company's VP of Product, and the Nagpur expansion had been her idea eight months earlier: Tier-2 cities, she had argued, were underserved, rents were a third of Pune's, and Girija Mart could get there before Blinkit did. The board had approved a pilot. The pilot had run for eleven weeks. The results sat in front of her now, and they were not what she had promised.

The headline number the finance team had circulated read well at first glance: Girija Mart's Pune dark stores were doing roughly 40,000 orders a day, gross merchandise value was growing 11 percent quarter over quarter, and the company's blended profit-and-loss statement showed narrowing losses. But Rohan Mehta, the CFO, had asked a sharper question in the Monday pre-read: not whether the company as a whole was moving in the right direction, but whether a single, ordinary order in Pune — and a single, ordinary order in the Nagpur pilot — made money on its own, stripped of every rupee of head-office salary, marketing campaign and warehouse lease that did not vary with that one order. If the answer was no for Pune, scaling Nagpur before fixing that would not spread the loss thinner. It would multiply it. Ananya had built the model her product managers used to size delivery-fee thresholds and promotion budgets; she knew, uneasily, that the answer to Rohan's question was not going to be a comfortable one. Before the board met on Thursday, she had two days to find out precisely where Girija Mart's unit economics stood, and precisely which lever, if pulled, would move it.

2. The idea: profit at the level of one transaction

Unit economics is the contribution margin earned or lost on a single unit of the business — one customer, one order, one subscription, one shipped item — once every cost that varies with that single unit has been subtracted from the revenue it generates, and before a single rupee of fixed overhead (office rent, the product team's salaries, brand marketing, the CEO's travel budget) has been allocated against it. It answers one narrow but decisive question: if this business served exactly one more unit tomorrow, with nothing else about the company changing, would that unit add money to the company or take money away from it? Contribution margin — the topic this one builds directly on — is simply that same subtraction, revenue minus variable cost, done once. Unit economics is what you get when you insist on doing that subtraction at the smallest meaningful unit of the business, order by order or customer by customer, rather than across the company's full income statement.

Nobody signs their name to "unit economics" the way Frederick Taylor signs his name to scientific management. The underlying arithmetic — separating costs that move with volume from costs that do not, so that a manager can see whether one more sale helps or hurts — is cost-volume-profit analysis, a staple of industrial and management accounting since American factory accountants formalized break-even analysis in the 1920s and 1930s. What changed was the audience and the vocabulary. During and after the dot-com collapse of 2000, venture investors who had watched e-commerce companies burn enormous sums without ever establishing that a single transaction was profitable began demanding the same order-level arithmetic from founders, and by the mid-2010s, as SaaS and consumer-internet investing matured, writers and investors such as Bill Gurley and David Skok had turned "unit economics" into standard venture vocabulary: a company could grow revenue impressively and still be worth nothing if each new unit of growth lost money. In India, the phrase became boardroom currency during the 2015–2023 e-commerce and quick-commerce funding cycle, when investors began asking a version of Rohan Mehta's question before every subsequent financing round: not "how big is the company," but "does one order, by itself, make sense?"

The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without flinching: "Unit economics is the profit or loss on one order once we strip out everything that doesn't vary with that order — it tells us whether growth is making us healthier or just making us bigger."

3. How it actually works: from one order to a formula

The mechanics begin with a decision that practitioners routinely skip past without naming: choosing the unit. For a subscription business the natural unit is usually the customer over some period; for a marketplace it is often the transaction or the order; for a manufacturer it might be the physical item shipped. Girija Mart's unit was the individual delivered order, because that was the level at which its costs actually varied — a rider is dispatched, a picker fills a bag, a payment is processed, once per order, regardless of whether the order contains two items or twenty.

The second step, and the one that separates people who genuinely understand unit economics from people who merely recite the term, is sorting every cost line into one of three buckets rather than two. Variable costs move roughly in proportion to the unit — the wholesale cost of the groceries themselves, the payment-gateway fee charged as a percentage of the order value. Fixed costs do not move with any individual unit at all — the software engineering team's salaries, the lease on the Pune head office, brand advertising on television. And in between sits a bucket most newcomers collapse into "variable" by mistake: semi-fixed or step costs, which are fixed for any one order but change in steps as volume crosses certain thresholds — a delivery rider's shift cost is roughly the same whether he carries a ₹300 basket or a ₹600 basket, but a whole additional rider must be added once order volume in a zone exceeds what the existing riders can carry. Unit economics, properly done, keeps the semi-fixed costs on the unit's ledger, because they are the costs the product team can actually influence order by order, even though they do not scale smoothly.

Once the costs are sorted, the arithmetic is genuinely simple: revenue per unit, minus every variable and semi-fixed cost attributable to that unit, equals contribution margin per unit. What is easy to miss is what happens next, which is where the implicit step lives: because most of a unit's costs are a mix of a cost that moves with the rupee value of the order (like COGS and payment fees, expressed as a percentage) and a cost that is roughly flat per order (like the rider's delivery cost), the contribution margin of a single order is not a fixed number — it is a straight line as a function of the order's size. That line has a slope, set by the percentage-of-revenue costs, and an intercept, set by the flat per-order costs. Finding where that line crosses zero — the average order value at which a single order stops losing money and starts making it — is the single most useful number a product manager pricing or packaging a transactional business can produce, and it is exactly what Ananya set out to calculate for Girija Mart's Pune orders.

4. The worked example: one order in Pune, then one order after a product change

Ananya pulled the average numbers for a typical Pune order in the week ending 5 April 2026. The average order value (AOV) — what the customer paid for the groceries themselves — was ₹420. Girija Mart bought that same basket of groceries from wholesalers and its own dark-store inventory for roughly 78 percent of what it sold it for, so the cost of goods sold (COGS) on a ₹420 order was ₹327.60. Packaging — bags, and for chilled items a reusable ice pack — cost the company a flat ₹8 per order. Getting the order from the dark store to the customer's door, once rider payout, fuel or EV charging, and idle time between deliveries were averaged across a shift, cost ₹58 per order, largely independent of basket size. The payment gateway charged 2 percent of the transaction value to process a digital payment, or ₹8.40. And because Girija Mart was still running a promotional discount to defend share against Zepto and Blinkit in the neighborhoods where all three competed, the average order carried ₹20 of discount, funded out of the company's own revenue.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Contribution margin is not gross margin, and confusing the two flatters the business

Gross margin, as accountants define it, typically subtracts only the cost of goods sold from revenue. Girija Mart's gross margin on that ₹420 order was a healthy-looking 22 percent. Its contribution margin, once delivery, packaging, payment fees and discounts were included, was negative. A team that reports gross margin in a board deck and calls it "unit economics" is not lying, but it is answering a much easier question than the one that matters, and every quick-commerce postmortem written about the 2021–2023 funding cycle turns on exactly this substitution.

The unit you choose changes the answer, and the choice is a judgment call

Girija Mart could have measured unit economics per order, per customer per month, or per item. Each answers a different question. Per-order economics tells a product manager whether today's transaction is healthy. Per-customer economics, folding in how often a customer orders and for how long they stay, is what connects unit economics to the next topic in this sequence, customer acquisition cost and lifetime value. Neither choice is wrong, but reporting one while a reader assumes the other is a common source of boardroom confusion.

Fixed, variable and semi-fixed are a spectrum, and misclassifying the middle is the most common technical error

A rider's per-shift cost looks fixed at the level of one order and variable at the level of a whole city's order volume, because it steps up in whole-rider increments once demand density crosses a threshold. Analysts who treat it as purely variable overstate how much unit economics will improve as volume grows in a new city; analysts who treat it as purely fixed understate how much it can be optimized through better routing and denser demand. Girija Mart's Nagpur pilot had assumed Pune-level delivery density from day one, when Nagpur's lower order density meant each rider actually covered fewer stops per hour.

A positive number here does not mean the company is profitable

Even after the checkout nudge lifted contribution margin to ₹18 per order, Girija Mart's total profit-and-loss statement still showed a large loss, because engineering salaries, warehouse leases, the marketing team and head-office rent were real costs that simply were not attributable to any single order. Positive unit economics is a necessary condition for a transactional business to eventually be profitable at scale; it is never a sufficient one. The company still needed enough order volume for that ₹18 per order, multiplied across every order, to exceed its fixed costs — a separate calculation entirely, usually called the fixed-cost break-even point, distinct from the per-unit break-even AOV in Figure 2.

Blending hides the cohort that is actually failing

The company-wide blended unit economics Girija Mart reported to its board averaged healthy, longstanding Pune neighborhoods together with the brand-new Nagpur pilot zones. The blend looked survivable. Nagpur alone, where basket sizes were smaller and delivery density lower, did not. A single blended number, however precisely calculated, can conceal exactly the sub-population a decision-maker most needs to see, which is why the discipline calls for reporting unit economics by cohort — by city, by acquisition channel, by customer vintage — before reporting it company-wide.

Promotions distort the number in both directions, and both distortions are dangerous

A discount funded by the company, like Girija Mart's ₹20 per order, depresses today's measured contribution margin and can make a genuinely good business look bad in a snapshot. The opposite trap is equally common: measuring unit economics only on full-price, non-promotional orders overstates how healthy the business actually is, since promotions are often how a meaningful share of real customers are won. The honest number is the blended one, discounts included, with the discount's cost made visible as its own line rather than netted quietly against revenue.

Unit economics tells you almost nothing about whether customers actually want the product

An order can be comfortably profitable and still belong to a company that is losing customers every month, because unit economics says nothing about retention, satisfaction or repeat behavior on its own. It measures the money in one transaction, not the durability of the relationship that produced it. A thoughtful reader confronted with a healthy unit-economics number should still ask a second, entirely separate question: how many of these transactions will this customer generate, and for how long — which is precisely why this topic unlocks lifetime value in the sequence that follows it.

The time window chosen for "variable" cost quietly changes the verdict

Over a single week, warehouse rent is fixed no matter how many orders pass through a dark store. Over three years, if volume forecasts justify opening a second dark store or closing an underused one, that same rent becomes a decision variable tied to volume. Every unit-economics calculation implicitly assumes a time horizon over which costs are being held fixed, and two analysts who disagree about a business's health are frequently just using different horizons without saying so.

6. How the picture changes by business model and by stage

In a pure consumer transaction business like Girija Mart, the unit economics conversation centers on exactly the levers this example used: basket size, delivery cost per trip, and discount intensity, because the company touches both the cost of the goods and the cost of getting them to the customer. B2B software businesses face a structurally different picture: consider Gitanjali CloudBooks, a Chennai-based accounting-software company selling to small manufacturers, where the "unit" is a subscribing company rather than an order, COGS is a small hosting cost per customer rather than 78 percent of revenue, and the dominant number on the cost side is the cost of the sales team required to close each account — so unit economics there is inseparable from the customer-acquisition-cost calculation this topic unlocks, rather than from delivery logistics. Marketplace businesses sit in yet a third position: Gopal Agri Exchange, which connects wheat and pulses traders in Punjab's mandis to flour mills and retailers, never owns the goods that move across its platform, so it has no COGS line at all — its unit economics are almost entirely a function of the commission rate it charges against gross transaction value, weighed against the cost of the verification and credit-guarantee infrastructure it must run to make traders trust a stranger on the other side of the trade.

Stage matters just as much as business model. At an early-stage company, unit economics is deliberately measured with a generous hand: fixed and semi-fixed costs that will shrink dramatically with scale — a single warehouse manager overseeing a half-empty dark store, a support team sized for far more volume than currently exists — are often reported separately from the "steady-state" unit economics the company expects once it reaches efficient scale, because collapsing the two together would make an investable early business look permanently broken. At a large, mature company, the opposite discipline applies: semi-fixed costs that once looked like rounding errors, spread across millions of units, become the difference between a healthy category and a loss-making one, and the fixed-versus-variable line must be redrawn far more strictly, with corporate overhead that a startup could reasonably ignore now allocated back down to the unit level for internal accountability. Girija Mart, seven years into its life and preparing to raise a growth round, was squarely in the uncomfortable middle: too large to wave away weak unit economics as a temporary artifact of scale, not yet large enough for the semi-fixed costs in a new city like Nagpur to have stepped down to their efficient level.

7. Common mistakes

The first and most frequent mistake is reporting gross margin while calling it unit economics, as described above; the symptom is a board deck where the unit-economics slide looks reassuring but the cash-burn slide two pages later does not, and the cheapest diagnostic is to list every cost line item the company actually incurs per order and check, one by one, whether it appears above or below the reported "margin" figure. The second is treating a genuinely semi-fixed cost as if it scales down automatically with growth, without evidence; the symptom is a forecast in which unit economics is projected to improve steadily as volume rises, and the diagnostic is to plot the actual historical cost per unit against actual historical volume and see whether the relationship is really as smooth as the forecast assumes, or whether it moves in discrete steps that a smooth trendline is papering over. The third is reporting a single blended number across meaningfully different cohorts, cities or channels; the symptom is a company-wide average that looks stable quarter over quarter while specific new markets or channels are quietly deteriorating underneath it, and the cheapest diagnostic is simply to slice the same calculation by cohort before presenting the average. The fourth, and the one Ananya's own early Nagpur model had committed, is calculating unit economics using assumptions carried over from a mature market without re-measuring them in the new one — delivery density, basket size and discount intensity all differ by city, and importing Pune's numbers into a Nagpur forecast quietly imports Pune's break-even point along with them, even though Nagpur's actual break-even point, given its lower order density, sat well above it.

8. What good looks like

Six months later, a different quick-commerce product team at a rival firm faced the same decision Girija Mart had faced in April, and handled it differently from the start. Before proposing expansion into a new city, that team built a unit-economics model with delivery density, average basket size and discount intensity as explicit, separately-sourced inputs for the target city rather than inherited assumptions from an existing one, and ran a two-week controlled test in a single neighborhood before committing capital to a citywide rollout. The test measured contribution margin directly, cohort by cohort, and reported it to the board alongside — not folded into — the company's blended, company-wide numbers, with the semi-fixed delivery cost broken out explicitly so that the board could see how many additional orders per rider-shift were needed to reach the city's true break-even AOV. When the new city's numbers came in below target, the team did not average the shortfall away; it delayed the wider rollout, tested a checkout-based basket-size nudge exactly as Girija Mart eventually did, and only scaled once the tested change had moved the measured, unblended cohort number across its break-even line. Nothing about that process was exotic. It simply refused to let a comfortable blended average, an inherited assumption, or a gross-margin figure stand in for the one number that actually mattered: does the marginal order here make money, on its own terms, today.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya walked into Thursday's board meeting with three numbers rather than one: the current Pune contribution margin of −₹2.00 per order, the projected ₹18.00 per order once the checkout nudge shipped everywhere, and Nagpur's own break-even AOV, recalculated with Nagpur's actual, lower delivery density rather than Pune's — which came out to ₹460, thirty rupees higher than Pune's, because each Nagpur rider covered fewer stops per hour. Her recommendation was not to cancel Nagpur, and not to scale it either. She proposed shipping the basket-size nudge in Pune first, where it could be tested against a large existing base within weeks, and holding the Nagpur rollout to its current handful of pilot stores until the nudge had been validated and then re-modeled specifically against Nagpur's own delivery-density numbers, not Pune's. Growth into a twelfth dark store, she told the board, was not currently a growth decision at all; it was a decision to multiply a loss she had only just learned how to see clearly. The board approved the narrower plan. Rohan Mehta's one comment, as the meeting closed, was the sentence Ananya intended to put above her own desk: a business does not become healthy by getting bigger before it is healthy.

What Ananya's team took up next, in the weeks that followed, was customer acquisition cost and lifetime value — because a positive contribution margin on one order says nothing about whether the customer who placed it was worth acquiring in the first place, and the same discount that depressed today's unit economics was also, potentially, an investment in a customer who would order fifty more times. That is the natural next question this topic hands off to the next one. Two questions are worth sitting with before it is asked: first, for any transactional business a reader is evaluating, what is the one input — basket size, delivery cost, take rate, churn — that the product team can actually move this quarter, and has anyone modeled how far it would need to move to cross the business's true break-even line? And second, when a company reports that its unit economics are improving, is the reader looking at one genuine cohort getting healthier, or at a blend in which a shrinking healthy cohort is simply outweighing a growing unhealthy one for one more quarter?

Two questions to sit with:
